days.title: Torch lands in North Africa
days.imageCredit: American troops debark from assault boats onto a North African beach, November 1942. U.S. Army Signal Corps SC 149955, public domain.
days.post:
In the U.S. Army's first large scale landing under fire, the men shooting back were French.

In the early morning darkness of 8 November 1942, American and British troops came ashore in French North Africa, around Casablanca, Oran, and Algiers. Nobody knew for certain whether the forces of Vichy France would fight. They did, hardest of all around Casablanca, where the unfinished battleship Jean Bart, with only one working turret, traded fire with USS Massachusetts.

Landing craft grounded on sandbars nobody had scouted, and vehicles failed in the surf. Most of the fighting was over in three days, but more than 1,300 Vichy French troops were killed.

Was North Africa the right place for America's first big landing, or a detour from the real war?
replies: Patton was aboard the cruiser USS Augusta. The landing boat he meant to take ashore was damaged by the blast of the cruiser's own 8 inch guns, and most of his luggage went overboard. Admiral Francois Darlan ordered French forces to stop resisting at noon on 10 November, and Casablanca surrendered on 11 November. The campaign cost the United States 556 dead and 837 wounded, and Britain 574 dead.

Photos: American troops debark from assault boats onto a North African beach, November 1942. U.S. Army Signal Corps SC 149955, public domain. On the card: American troops in a landing craft heading for the beaches at Oran, Algeria, November 1942. Imperial War Museum A 12661, public domain.

Sources: Operation Torch, Wikipedia; Learning the Lessons of Victory, U.S. Army; Naval Battle of Casablanca, Wikipedia; Encyclopaedia Britannica; French battleship Jean Bart, Wikipedia; U.S. National Archives.
days.alt: Archival photo of American soldiers in helmets wading ashore through shallow water from a landing craft, rifles in hand, with a transport ship faint in the haze behind them.
facts: 8 November 1942, early morning darkness: Operation Torch begins.
About 107,000 Allied troops, landing around Casablanca, Oran, and Algiers.
Western Task Force: about 35,000 Americans under Patton, sailed straight from Hampton Roads, Virginia.
Vichy French forces fought, hardest around Casablanca.
Jean Bart, unfinished, one working turret, traded fire with USS Massachusetts.
The U.S. Army's first large scale amphibious landing under hostile fire.
Darlan ordered a stop to resistance at noon on 10 November; Casablanca surrendered 11 November.
Losses: U.S. 556 dead and 837 wounded, Britain 574 dead, more than 1,300 Vichy French killed.

days.title: Patton attacks in the rain
days.imageCredit: A tank moves up a tree lined road near Delme, Lorraine, 9 November 1944. Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2678 (NARA 16482), public domain.
days.post:
In Lorraine that November, trench foot put almost as many American soldiers out of action as enemy fire did.

On 8 November 1944, Patton's Third Army opened a new offensive toward Metz and the German border. The weather was so bad the Germans thought nobody would attack, so the assault caught them by surprise. XII Corps opened with 540 guns firing 22,000 rounds, and early on 9 November the 90th Infantry Division crossed the swollen Moselle at Koenigsmacker.

Then the rain kept coming. Seven inches fell that month, about twice the normal amount, the worst flooding in 35 years. Mud and cloud cost the Americans much of their air advantage, with no air activity at all on 12 days.

Was attacking in that weather bold generalship, or a gamble the infantry paid for?
replies: The weather was so bad that Maj. Gen. Manton Eddy of XII Corps asked Patton to postpone. Patton told him to attack as scheduled or name his successor. The water ran so high that five days passed before armor could cross the Moselle there in force. Third Army closed the ring around Metz on 19 November, and the Lorraine campaign cost it 55,182 combat casualties.

Photos: A tank moves up a tree lined road near Delme, Lorraine, 9 November 1944. Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2678 (NARA 16482), public domain. On the card: Jeeps of the 4th Armored Division drive through the ruins of Dieuze, Lorraine, November 1944. U.S. Army photo, from The Lorraine Campaign (U.S. Army Center of Military History), public domain.

Sources: Christopher R. Gabel, The Lorraine Campaign: An Overview, Combat Studies Institute; Battle of Metz and Lorraine campaign, Wikipedia; U.S. National Archives.
days.alt: Still from wartime film of an American tank with men riding on top, moving down a muddy road lined with bare trees, with more vehicles in the distance.
facts: 8 November 1944: Third Army opens its new offensive in Lorraine, aimed at Metz.
Eddy asked to postpone; Patton said attack as scheduled or name your successor.
Germans thought the weather too bad for an attack, so they were surprised.
Biggest artillery preparation in Third Army history: 42 battalions, 540 guns, 22,000 rounds.
9 November: 90th Infantry Division crosses the swollen Moselle at Koenigsmacker.
Seven inches of rain that November, rain on 20 days, worst flooding in 35 years.
Trench foot put almost as many men out of action as enemy fire.
Ring around Metz closed 19 November; last fort held out until 13 December.

days.title: Ike in the mud
days.imageCredit: Eisenhower with Lt. Gen. William H. Simpson and Maj. Gen. Raymond McLain in a jeep on the way to the front, November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo SC 196509, Eisenhower Presidential Library, public domain.
days.post:
Operation Queen had already been put off twice by the weather when the Supreme Allied Commander went to see the men who would make it.

On 10 November 1944, Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower went to the Ninth Army front on the German and Dutch border. At Herzogenrath he climbed out of his jeep and pulled off his raincoat. Near Eigelshoven he walked a muddy wood and stood in the fallen leaves, hands on hips, talking with men of the 29th Infantry Division.

Queen opened on 16 November behind 1,204 American heavy bombers. The Americans reached the Roer River in about a month of hard fighting, but could not cross it before the Germans struck in the Ardennes.

Did visits like this really matter to the men in the mud, or were they mostly for the cameras?
replies: Riding with him were Lt. Gen. Omar Bradley, Lt. Gen. William H. Simpson of the Ninth Army, and Maj. Gen. Raymond McLain of XIX Corps. The 29th and 30th Infantry Divisions and the 2nd Armored Division led the Ninth Army's part of Queen. The Ninth Army alone lost 1,133 killed, 6,864 wounded, and 2,059 missing.

Photos: Eisenhower with Lt. Gen. William H. Simpson and Maj. Gen. Raymond McLain in a jeep on the way to the front, November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo SC 196509, Eisenhower Presidential Library, public domain. On the card: Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower talks to men of the 29th Infantry Division at the front, 10 November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, NARA 111-SC-196364, public domain.

Sources: U.S. National Archives (Signal Corps film and photos); Operation Queen, Wikipedia; Eisenhower Presidential Library.
days.alt: Archival photo of Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower in a peaked cap and fur collared coat sitting in the back of a mud spattered jeep, with a helmeted general behind him.
facts: 10 November 1944: Eisenhower visits the Ninth Army front on the German and Dutch border.
At Herzogenrath he was greeted by Maj. Gen. Leland Hobbs of the 30th Infantry Division.
With him: Bradley, Simpson (Ninth Army), and McLain (XIX Corps).
Near Eigelshoven he talked with men of the 2nd Battalion, 175th Infantry, 29th Division.
Queen's start had slipped from 5 November and then from 10 November.
16 November: 1,204 American heavy bombers dropped 4,120 bombs ahead of the attack.
Ninth Army losses: 1,133 killed, 6,864 wounded, 2,059 missing.

days.title: Churchill and de Gaulle in Paris
days.imageCredit: De Gaulle talks with Churchill at the saluting base, with Anthony Eden, Paris, 11 November 1944. IWM BU 1294, public domain.
days.post:
Just weeks after Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union recognized de Gaulle's government, he and Churchill rode up the Champs-Elysees side by side.

On Armistice Day, 11 November 1944, less than three months after Paris was freed, the two men set out at 10:45 a.m. in open cars, across the Seine and through the Place de la Concorde. Parisians packed the sidewalks, windows, and rooftops, chanting "Vive de Gaulle! Vive Churchill!"

At the Arc de Triomphe they laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and stood through a minute of silence, then watched an hour long parade of French, British, American, Canadian, Moroccan, and Algerian troops.

Was this day more about honoring the dead, or about showing the world who now led France?

Today is Veterans Day. If there's a veteran you're remembering, share their name below.

#VeteransDay
replies: Churchill had landed at Orly the afternoon before with his wife Clementine and daughter Mary, and de Gaulle met them with a guard of honor. Some of his cabinet had tried to talk him out of going, since German stragglers were thought to be hiding in the city. At lunch afterward, with tears in his eyes, he said it gave him great pleasure "to see Paris again, this Paris which is a brilliant star shining above the world."

Photos: De Gaulle talks with Churchill at the saluting base, with Anthony Eden, Paris, 11 November 1944. IWM BU 1294, public domain. On the card: Winston Churchill and Charles de Gaulle walk down the Champs-Elysees, Paris, 11 November 1944. Imperial War Museum BU 1292, public domain.

Sources: The Churchill Project, Hillsdale College; U.S. National Archives; New Zealand Herald, 13 November 1944, Papers Past; Provisional Government of the French Republic, Wikipedia.
days.alt: Archival photo of Winston Churchill in an RAF greatcoat and cap seated beside Charles de Gaulle in uniform, who leans in to talk, with Anthony Eden on the right and officers and officials packed behind them.
facts: 11 November 1944, Armistice Day, less than three months after Paris was freed.
Recognition of de Gaulle's Provisional Government by Britain, the U.S., and the USSR: 23 October 1944.
10:45 a.m.: open cars from the War Ministry, across the Seine, through the Concorde, up the avenue.
Crowds chanted "Vive de Gaulle! Vive Churchill!" Churchill gave his V sign.
Wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a minute of silence at the salute.
Hour long parade: French, British, American, Canadian, Moroccan, and Algerian troops.
Some of Churchill's cabinet tried to talk him out of going.

days.title: The Tirpitz goes down
days.imageCredit: The capsized Tirpitz in the fjord near Tromso, attended by salvage vessels, 22 March 1945. RAF reconnaissance photo, No. 544 Squadron, public domain.
days.post:
Britain tried for years to sink one battleship: with midget submarines in September 1943, carrier dive bombers in April 1944, and heavy bombers that September.

On the morning of 12 November 1944, RAF Lancasters of No. 9 and No. 617 Squadrons, led by Wing Commander J. B. Tait, attacked Tirpitz near Tromso, each carrying a single 12,000 pound Tallboy. The run began at 09:35. At least two bombs hit her directly, and within minutes she was listing hard. After a magazine exploded, she rolled over and capsized.

Somewhere between about 950 and 1,204 German sailors died. Men trapped inside the upturned hull were cut free through her exposed bottom, and 82 were rescued that way.
replies: Tirpitz displaced about 42,900 tonnes and carried eight 15 inch guns. She had hardly fought, but simply by existing she forced the Royal Navy to keep powerful forces in home waters to watch her. With her gone, the last German battleship threat to the Arctic convoys and the North Atlantic was over.

Photos: The capsized Tirpitz in the fjord near Tromso, attended by salvage vessels, 22 March 1945. RAF reconnaissance photo, No. 544 Squadron, public domain. On the card: RAF air photo of the attack on the Tirpitz near Tromso, Norway, 12 November 1944. Imperial War Museum C 4775, public domain.

Sources: German battleship Tirpitz, Wikipedia; Target the Tirpitz, RAF Museum; List of Allied attacks on Tirpitz, Wikipedia; Australian War Memorial film C189542; Bomber Command Museum of Canada.
days.alt: Archival aerial photo of the battleship Tirpitz lying upside down in a fjord, her long hull showing above the water with small salvage vessels alongside, snow covering the shore.
facts: 12 November 1944, near Tromso, Norway.
Lancasters of No. 9 and No. 617 Squadrons, led by Wing Commander J. B. Tait.
Between 29 and 32 bombers, each with one 12,000 pound Tallboy.
Run began 09:35. At least two direct hits; a magazine exploded and she capsized.
About 950 to 1,204 German sailors died; the RAF Museum says about a thousand.
82 men were cut free through the upturned hull.
Earlier attempts: midget submarines (Sept 1943), carrier dive bombers (April 1944), Tallboys (Sept 1944).
A No. 463 Squadron RAAF film crew flew with the raid.

days.title: Halsey's carriers hit Manila again
days.imageCredit: Smoke rises over the Manila waterfront during the carrier strike, 13 November 1944. Still from U.S. Navy film Strike on Manila Bay Area (428-NPC-6221, NARA 77801), public domain.
days.post:
The light cruiser Kiso had orders to leave Manila Bay for Brunei that evening, carrying Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima and his staff. She never got out.

On 13 November 1944, carrier planes of Admiral Halsey's Task Force 38 struck Japanese shipping in and around the bay, and more than 350 of them went after Kiso as she got under way. Between about 8:00 and 9:23 a.m., three bombs hit her. She lost power and settled into the shallow water west of Cavite.

At Cavite, the destroyers Akishimo and Akebono were moored side by side when bombs set both ablaze. A huge explosion aboard Akishimo the next day wrecked them both.

Was sending more than 350 planes after one light cruiser smart overkill, or wasted effort?
replies: The bombs struck Kiso in the bow, near the boiler rooms, and near the aft guns. Accounts of her losses differ: Pacific Wrecks gives 89 killed and 105 wounded, while another count says 175 men went down with her and 104 survived. Japan salvaged her wreck in 1955 and broke her up for scrap in 1956.

Photos: Smoke rises over the Manila waterfront during the carrier strike, 13 November 1944. Still from U.S. Navy film Strike on Manila Bay Area (428-NPC-6221, NARA 77801), public domain. On the card: The wreck of the Japanese destroyer Okinami, sunk on 13 November 1944, in Manila Bay, February 1945. U.S. Navy photo, Naval History and Heritage Command, public domain.

Sources: Japanese cruiser Kiso, Wikipedia; Kiso, Pacific Wrecks; Japanese destroyer Akishimo, Wikipedia; U.S. National Archives.
days.alt: Still from wartime aerial film of a waterfront seen across a wide bay, with two dark columns of smoke rising into a hazy sky.
facts: 13 November 1944: Task Force 38 strikes shipping in and around Manila Bay.
More than 350 carrier planes went after the light cruiser Kiso.
Carriers included Hornet, Essex, Ticonderoga, Enterprise, and four light carriers.
Kiso was to leave for Brunei that evening with Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima and staff.
Three bombs between about 8:00 and 9:23 a.m.; she settled west of Cavite.
Akishimo and Akebono, moored side by side, both wrecked.
Destroyer Okinami and transports also sunk that day.
Kiso salvaged 1955, scrapped 1956.

days.title: Patton crosses the Moselle
days.imageCredit: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton with Maj. Gen. Walton Walker and Brig. Gen. James Van Fleet at Koenigsmacker, 14 November 1944. Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2688 (NARA 16492), public domain.
days.post:
The engineers blasting their way into Fort Koenigsmacker used so much explosive that more had to be dropped to them by air.

The fort, built by the Germans between 1908 and 1915, had four 100 mm guns in revolving armored turrets. Early on 9 November 1944, the 90th Infantry Division crossed the Moselle opposite it in assault boats at the height of a flood, where the water was almost a mile wide. The fort's fire wrecked bridging equipment and harried the men in the boats.

On 14 November, Patton crossed to see the bridgehead for himself, riding in an armored car, then touring the freed town by jeep.

Patton called it an epic river crossing. Does it deserve a place beside the war's famous crossings?
replies: Taking the fort cost about 111 American casualties, and more than 300 Germans were killed, wounded, or captured. On the night of 11 to 12 November, the 25th Panzergrenadier Division counterattacked at Kerling with about ten tanks and assault guns, and failed. The bridgehead was the northern arm of a pincer, and Third Army closed the ring around Metz on 19 November.

Photos: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton with Maj. Gen. Walton Walker and Brig. Gen. James Van Fleet at Koenigsmacker, 14 November 1944. Still from U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2688 (NARA 16492), public domain. On the card: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton at the 80th Infantry Division command post in Lorraine, 3 November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, NARA 111-SC-196153, public domain.

Sources: U.S. National Archives (Signal Corps film); Raymond E. Bell Jr., Patton's Fight for Fort Koenigsmacker, WWII Quarterly; Fort de Koenigsmacker, Wikipedia; Gabel, The Lorraine Campaign; Battle of Metz, Wikipedia.
days.alt: Still from wartime film of Lt. Gen. George S. Patton, three stars on his helmet, in a belted trench coat, standing with two helmeted generals in front of a battered stone building.
facts: 14 November 1944: Patton visits the 90th Division bridgehead at Koenigsmacker.
With him: Maj. Gen. Walton Walker (XX Corps) and Brig. Gen. James Van Fleet (90th Division).
Crossing began 3:30 a.m. on 9 November; four waves of 40 assault boats followed.
River almost a mile wide opposite the fort, in places four feet deep.
Fort Koenigsmacker: built 1908 to 1915, four 100 mm guns in armored turrets.
Garrison gave up on 11 or 12 November; accounts differ.
About 111 American casualties; more than 300 Germans killed, wounded, or captured.
Ring around Metz closed 19 November.
